Besotted means being so deeply and intensely in love with, or fascinated by, someone or something that you lose your ability to think clearly or see their flaws. You are completely under their spell. Your feelings are so overwhelming that they practically take over your rational mind.

The single most important preposition that goes with this word is "with" — you are besotted with someone or something.

Think of it this way: when a normal person likes someone, they can still see that person's faults. But when someone is besotted, they are so far gone in their feelings that they are almost blind to reality. The world could be telling them "this person is terrible for you" and they simply wouldn't care — or wouldn't even register it. That level of helpless, consuming devotion is what besotted captures.

It is stronger than simply being "in love." It carries a sense of being almost stupefied, dazed, or intoxicated by your feelings. Your judgment is clouded. Your critical thinking is switched off. You are, in a word, gone.
Who or What Can You Be Besotted With?

1. A Person (most common use)

This is the classic use. It almost always implies romantic feelings — deep infatuation, love, or obsession with another person.

"He was completely besotted with her from the moment they met."
(He fell so hard and so fast that he couldn't think straight.)

"She knew he was besotted with her — he agreed with everything she said and laughed at every joke, even the bad ones."
(He was so in love that his judgment was gone.)

"The young actor became besotted with his co-star during filming."

2. A Thing, Idea, or Hobby

You can also be besotted with a non-person — a passion, a place, an idea, a hobby. In this case it means you are completely, irrationally consumed by it.

"She is utterly besotted with vintage fashion — she spends every weekend hunting for old clothes."

"The writer was so besotted with the idea that he couldn't stop working on it, even at 3 AM."

"Ever since their trip, the whole family has been besotted with Italy."
The Emotional Tone of the Word

This is important: besotted is not a neutral word. It carries a specific emotional color depending on who is using it and how.

  • When used by an observer about someone else, it often has a slightly amused, gentle, or teasing tone — as if the speaker is smiling at someone who has clearly lost their senses over another person. It is not cruel or harsh, but it does gently acknowledge that the besotted person's judgment is impaired.

    "Look at him — he's absolutely besotted. He hasn't stopped talking about her for three weeks."

  • When used to describe oneself, it feels like an honest, self-aware confession — admitting that your feelings are bigger than your reason.

    "I'll be honest, I was completely besotted. I couldn't see a single thing wrong with him."

  • In both cases, the word is never cold or clinical. It always feels warm, human, and emotionally charged.

It helps to see where besotted sits compared to similar words, from milder to stronger:

fond of → attracted to → in love with → infatuated with → smitten with → besotted with → obsessed with

Besotted sits near the intense end. It is stronger than "in love" (which is straightforward and clear-headed) and stronger than "infatuated" (which is already strong). It is just a small step below obsessed, but unlike "obsessed," besotted keeps a warm, even charming feeling — obsession sounds darker and more dangerous. Besotted sounds human and relatable.
Key Modifiers You'll See With It

Writers and speakers almost always intensify besotted with adverbs, because the word invites emphasis:

  • Utterly besotted (completely, totally)
  • Completely besotted
  • Hopelessly besotted (in a way that suggests there's no coming back)
  • Absolutely besotted
  • Totally besotted
  • Deeply besotted

"Hopelessly besotted" is a particularly beloved combination — it adds the sense that the person knows they've lost control but cannot do anything about it.

In older English, besotted also meant being stupefied or dulled in the mind by alcohol (a "sot" was an old word for a drunkard). While this meaning is now rare and mostly archaic, knowing it helps you feel why the word feels the way it does — the idea of being so overwhelmed by something that you lose your grip on reason is baked right into the word's bones. When someone is besotted with a person today, the implication is the same: their senses are gone, they are intoxicated — just by love rather than liquor.

• It is not casual. You don't say "I'm a bit besotted." The word demands intensity.
  • It is not hateful or sinister. Even when used with a teasing tone, it's affectionate.
  • It is not the same as admiration. You can admire someone with a perfectly clear head. Besotted implies you've lost your clear head.
  • It is not temporary infatuation only. While infatuation is often short-lived, besotted can describe a long, deep, lasting state of devotion.
One Final Image to Remember It By

Imagine someone staring across a room at the person they love, completely unaware that their coffee is getting cold, that their friend is calling their name, or that they've been standing there for ten minutes. They have a soft, slightly dazed look on their face. They are, simply, not fully in this world anymore.

That person is besotted.
